drills.coachNote: Black's king is looking to run toward e7 and d6 to blockade and eventually attack your c6-pawn, and every tempo you waste lets it get there. Bb3 doesn't touch f7, so it hands over exactly that tempo — after Ke7, Kc4, Kf7 you've let the king get active before you finally correct with Ba2, costing you a big chunk of your advantage. Ba2 was right immediately: it sits on the a2-g8 diagonal, controlling f7 and repeatedly nudging the black king back, so your own king strolls to b5 unopposed (Ke7 Kc4 Ke8 Kb5 Kd8) to escort your pawns home. In king-and-pawn endings, use your bishop to control key squares in front of the enemy king, not just develop it.
drills.threat: Black's king wants to march to e7-d6 and start hassling your advanced c6-pawn while your bishop sits idle.

drills.coachNote: Black wants Qxd2#: the queen swoops in on the g5-d2 diagonal, and with your rook on f2 blocked and no escape on d1 or e2, it's instant mate. Rf1 walks straight into it — it doesn't defend d2 at all, and it even clogs f1, taking away your king's last escape square, so Qxd2# landed immediately and ended a game where you were up over five pawns with your queen buried deep on c8. Qd7+ was the move: it's check first, kicking the black king to f6, which buys you the tempo to finally castle queenside with O-O-O and tuck your king away safely before continuing the attack. When your own king is this exposed, always check for forcing moves that fix your king safety before making a quiet developing move.

drills.coachNote: Black never castled, so the g6-f7-e8 diagonal runs straight into his king, and his rook on h5 is just sitting there unprotected — a checking move that hits both would be devastating. Qd4 ignores all of that, just centralizing, so black calmly plays Qd7, then swings in with Bf4, Qh7, and even Qa4+ with tempo — the initiative flips to him and your advantage bleeds away. Qg6+ was the shot: check along that open diagonal forces the king to move (Kd7), and then Qxh5 simply scoops up the undefended rook for free, e.g. Kc6 Nd4+ Kb7 and you're up a full rook with black's king still stuck in the center. Whenever the enemy king hasn't castled, scan the open diagonals into it before reaching for a quiet move.

drills.coachNote: White's whole plan is to get his king to d5 or c5 so it can shepherd the a6 and b6 pawns forward, and any spare tempo you hand him speeds that up. Rc4+ did exactly that — after Kd5 the white king is already marching toward its pawns, and by the time you regroup with Rc3, the b-pawn runs to b7 and you're chasing a pawn that's nearly home, costing you nearly four pawns of eval in a position you were winning. Rc1 was the idea instead: it puts your rook behind the pawns rather than giving away a check the king is happy to receive, so once b7 goes through you're ready with Re1+, forcing the king back and getting your rook to b1 to blockade for good. In rook endings, a check that pushes the enemy king toward its own passed pawn is helping your opponent, not you.

Ra7 was the fix: it attacks the a6-pawn head-on, forcing White to babysit it with Re8 instead of pushing, which buys you time to march your own king in with Kd6 and start eating his kingside pawns. That leaves you with just a knight against a rook, the worst possible version of this ending, and the position collapses from merely uncomfortable to close to lost. g4 avoids the whole issue: it leaves the rook on the board, grabs kingside space, and keeps you fighting with Rd5 and Rc5 rather than volunteering into a hopeless minor-piece ending.
